Introduction: A thyristor (Silicon Controlled Rectifier, SCR) is a three-terminal, four-layer (PNPN) semiconductor device that behaves as a controlled switch. When the anode is positive with respecttothecathode,thedeviceremainsintheforward-blocking(off)stateandnosignificant current flows, even though it is forward biased, until a suitable trigger signal is applied to the gate terminal. As the gate-to-cathode voltage is increased, a corresponding gate current flows; once this reaches the gate trigger voltage/current (VGT/IGT), the thyristor switches into the forward-conduction (on) state. In this state, the anode-to-cathode voltage (VAK) collapses from nearly the full supply voltage to a small forward voltage drop, and the device continues to conduct even if the gate signal is removed, until the anode current falls below the holding current. This experiment studies this triggering behaviour by varying the gate voltage with a potentiometer and observing the corresponding change in VAK on a storage oscilloscope, in ordertoidentifythe gate voltage at whichtriggeringoccurs. Solar (PV) Plant Application 6.1 Why the Buck-Boost Converter is Preferred The terminal voltage of a photovoltaic (PV) panel changes considerably with solar irradiance and cell temperature. Depending on the conditions, the panel voltage V can be above or pv below the voltage required by the battery or DC bus. A buck converter can only step down and a boost converter can only step up, so neither can cover both situations. The buck-boost converter can, and for this reason it is preferred for the PV interface. (The inverted output polarity is not a problem for a DC bus or battery, as it only requires a reversed connection or an additional inverting stage.) 6.2 PV Source Model A PV panel is modelled by the single-diode equivalent circuit. Objectives: 1. To generate a signal of specified frequency using Timer0 of the ATmega32 microcontroller. 2. To understand the configuration and usage of Timer0 in the ATmega32 microcontroller for frequency generation. 3. To simulate the 1 Hz output in Proteus and validate the waveform using a virtual oscilloscope or by observing LED blinking. Theory: Timers of Atmega32 [1]: In the AVR ATmega16 / ATmega32 microcontrollers, there are three timers: Timer0, Timer1, and Timer2. These are 8bit, 16bit and 8bit respectively. Key Registers of Timer0 1. TCNT0: Timer / Counter Register 0 = It is an 8-bit register. It counts up with each pulse. 2. TCCR0: Timer / Counter Control Register 0 = This is an 8-bit register used for the operation mode and the clock source selection TCCR0 - Timer Control Resister 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 FOC0 WGM00 COM01 COM00 WGM01 CS02 CS01 CS00 Table 1: Timer Control Register TCCR0 Bits: 1. Bit 7 - FOC0: Force Compare Match: This write-only bit is used for forcing a compare match, useful in waveform generation. 2. Bit 6, 3 - WGM00, WGM01: Waveform Generation Mode WGM00 WGM01 Timer0 mode selection bit 0 0 Normal 0 1 CTC 1 0 Phase correct PWM 1 1 Fast PWM Table 2: Wave Generation Control Register Timer Modes: o Normal Mode: The timer counts from 0 to 255 and then overflows, resetting to 0. The overflow can trigger an interrupt. o CTC Mode (Clear timer on Compare Match): The timer counts up to a value specified in the OCR0 (Output Compare Register 0) and then resets to 0. The compare match can trigger an interrupt. o PWM Mode: Timer counts up and then down, providing a symmetric waveform. Useful for smoother motor control. The duty cycle is controlled by the value in OCR0. o Fast PWM Mode: Timer counts up to a maximum value and then resets, providing a faster switching frequency. 3. Bit 5:4 - COM01:00: Compare Output Mode These bits control the waveform generator. We will see this in the compare mode of the timer. 4. Bit 2:0 - CS02:CS00: Clock Source Select These bits are used to select a clock source. When CS02: CS00 = 000, then timer is stopped. As it gets a value between 001 to 101, it gets a clock source and starts as the timer. Table of Clock Source Select | CS02 | CS01 | CS00 | | |

As Bangladesh's renewable energy targets and planned solar parks come online, and as the national grid modernises toward smart-grid operation, power electronic converters will play an increasingly central role in closing the demand-supply gap sustainably rather than through further fossil-fuel capacity additions. Discussion: In this experiment, a Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controller was designed and implemented for a given linear system using both MATLAB and Simulink. The LQG controller combines a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) with a Kalman filter to provide optimal control under noisy conditions. The Kalman filter estimates the internal states from noisy outputs, while the LQR uses these estimates to generate the control input. The experiment demonstrated that the closed-loop system achieved better stability and performance compared to the open-loop response. Simulation results validated the theoretical expectations, showing an improved step response and confirming system stability (T = 1). Conclusion: The experiment successfully demonstrated the design and implementation of an LQG controller for a linear system. By integrating the Kalman filter with LQR, the controller effectively estimated the system states and stabilized the system despite measurement noise. Both MATLAB and Simulink simulations confirmed that the closed-loop system provided improved dynamic performance and ensured system stability. Objectives • To simulate and analyze latching circuits using FluidSIM, exploring their functionality and applications in pneumatic systems. • To study and understand the working principles of On Delay and Off Delay pneumatic timers, and their impact on system operation. • To implement and observe the behavior of A+B+A−B− and A+A−B+B− logic sequencing circuits in pneumatic systems, demonstrating their sequence control. • To demonstrate and investigate counter operations within pneumatic systems, highlighting their use in various automated processes. Theory In pneumatics, various components are used to control the sequence and timing of actuator operations. Latching Circuit: Latching was used to maintain the actuator’s state even after the control signal was removed. A self-holding circuit was built using a push-button and a directional control valve. On Delay Timer (Normally Closed Time Delay Valve): An On Delay Timer was used to delay the extension of an actuator after a signal was given. A normally closed (NC) time delay valve was used for this purpose. The valve only allowed air through after a preset time [1]. Off Delay Timer (Normally Open Time Delay Valve): An Off Delay Timer delayed the retraction of an actuator after the signal was removed. A normally open (NO) time delay valve was used, which closed after a set time, allowing the actuator to remain extended momentarily [1]. A+B+A−B− Sequencing: This sequencing involved extending cylinder A, followed by cylinder B. Then cylinder A retracted, followed by the retraction of cylinder B. It was achieved using roller lever valves and logical sequencing. A+A−B+B− Sequencing: This sequence required cylinder A to extend and retract first, then cylinder B to extend and retract. This ensured the complete action of one actuator before the other started. Counter Operations: Counters were used to control the number of cycles an actuator performed. When the pre-set count was reached, the operation was halted automatically. Fig 2: It successfully rotates the servo after entering correct password Discussion: The keypad works using a row-column scanning method. The microcontroller sets one row low at a time and reads column inputs. If a key is pressed, the corresponding column becomes low, allowing detection of the pressed key. The LCD receives commands and data through the lcd.h library, simplifying control operations such as initialization, cursor positioning, and character display. Using Arduino as a burner (ISP) eliminates the need for a dedicated programmer, making the system cost-effective and flexible. Challenges faced may include: Key debounce issues, Incorrect wiring of rows and columns, Timing mismatch in LCD initialization. The system integrates input (keypad), processing (ATmega32), and output (LCD + servo motor) into a complete embedded application. The keypad uses row-column scanning to detect pressed keys. The entered password is stored and compared using strcmp(). The LCD provides real-time feedback to the user. The servo motor is controlled using PWM generated by Timer1 of ATmega32. If the password matches: Servo rotates (unlock position). If incorrect: System denies access and remains locked and start to sound beep. Important considerations: Proper PWM calibration for servo angles are really tough to set. Debouncing keypad input was control from inside and 1k ohm resistance were attached. For secure password storage I added a shift bit so normally it’s unknown to others. Conclusion: The experiment successfully demonstrated how to interface a 4×4 keypad with ATmega32 and display inputs on an LCD. It enhanced understanding of input scanning techniques, LCD interfacing, and microcontroller programming using Arduino as ISP. The project reinforces several important concepts in embedded systems engineering, including GPIO configuration, peripheral interfacing, keypad matrix scanning, interrupt or polling-based sensor reading, software debouncing, and real-time display output using segment lookup tables. The modular firmware design allows for straightforward modification and extension of the system. The experiment successfully demonstrates a password-based door locking system using ATmega32. It combines: Human interaction (keypad), Processing logic (microcontroller), Mechanical actuation (servo motor). This system is widely used in: Smart homes, Office security systems, Electronic safes. It provides a strong foundation for building advanced IoT- based security systems in the future. In conclusion, this project serves as a well-rounded example of embedded system design that combines hardware interfacing, firmware logic, and practical utility. It demonstrates that even a modest 32-bit microcontroller, when properly programmed and interfaced, is capable of implementing responsive and reliable multi-input control

Theory: A controlled single-phase SCR (Silicon Controlled Rectifier) operates by using a gate triggering pulse to control the conduction period in an AC circuit. The phase-control thyristor remains in a non- conducting state until a gate pulse is applied, at which point it turns on and conducts current until the AC voltage crosses zero and the current falls below the holding level and is turned off due to natural or line commutation. This report examines the role of power electronics in environmental sustainability by discussing its fundamental features, key applications, recent technological developments, market trends, future prospects, and its growing significance in Bangladesh. Power-electronic converters and inverters are central to integrating renewable energy sources such as solar and wind into modern power systems, improving the efficiency of industrial motor drives, supporting energy storage, and enabling the adoption of electric vehicles. Recent advances in wide-bandgap semiconductors, particularly silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN), have pushed converter efficiencies beyond 98 percent [9]–[11]. In Bangladesh, renewable energy currently accounts for only a small share of total power generation; however, national policy targets and real-time grid data analyzed in this report indicate that power- electronic technologies will be essential for expanding solar capacity, stabilizing the grid, and meeting the country's 2030 and 2041 renewable-energy targets. Introduction Climate change, together with the continuous growth of global electricity demand, has made efficient energy generation, transmission, and utilization one of the greatest engineering challenges of this century. Power electronics — the conversion and control of electrical power using devices such as diodes, thyristors, MOSFETs, and IGBTs — has become central to addressing this challenge, as nearly every stage of a modern power system now passes through some form of electronic conversion [2]. Beyond conventional motor drives and uninterruptible power supplies, power electronics is now indispensable for integrating renewable sources, electric vehicles, HVDC transmission, and smart grids, all of which rely on converters for voltage regulation, frequency control, and grid synchronization [3]. This report presents a study of the fundamental features of power electronics, its contribution to renewable-energy integration, recent developments in wide-bandgap semiconductors, global market trends, and the current situation and future prospects in Bangladesh, supported by up-to- date generation and demand data obtained from the Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (PGCB). Key Features of Power Electronics for Sustainability Power-electronic converters transfer electrical energy from one stage of the power system to the next while allowing voltage, frequency, and waveform to be controlled with flexibility. Bangladesh Perspective Bangladesh's power sector remains heavily dependent on imported natural gas, furnace oil, and coal. Nonetheless, power electronics has already enabled significant progress through the Solar Home System (SHS) programme, one of the world's largest off-grid solar initiatives, which uses charge controllers, DC–DC converters, and small inverters to electrify millions of rural households that lack access to the national grid [17], [21]. The draft Renewable Energy Policy 2025 targets 20 percent renewable electricity by 2030 and 30 percent by 2041 [16], [18], requiring an estimated investment of USD 35–42.6 billion between 2025 and 2040 [18]. Key challenges include limited grid infrastructure, land-acquisition delays, heavy import-dependence for inverters and converters, outstanding payments exceeding USD 2.2 billion owed to independent power producers, and a shortage of skilled power-electronics engineers [18], [19]. Strengthening local manufacturing, MPPT-based solar systems, grid- connected converters, and technical education will therefore be critical to meeting these targets while improving grid reliability and energy security. Conclusion Power electronics has evolved into a fundamental component of modern sustainable energy systems, enabling renewable-energy integration, efficient industrial drives, electric vehicles, HVDC transmission, and battery storage. Wide-bandgap devices such as SiC and GaN now achieve conversion efficiencies exceeding 98 percent, and the global market for power electronics in renewable energy continues to expand steadily, reflecting growing investment in clean-energy technologies and electrification. For Bangladesh, the real-time PGCB data analyzed in this report confirm that, despite generation exceeding 13,000–16,000 MW, the grid still experiences substantial peak-hour load shedding and remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, with renewable sources contributing only a small and variable share. Meeting the country's 2030 and 2041 renewable-energy targets will require expanded generation capacity together with reliable power-electronic infrastructure — efficient inverters, converters, charge controllers, HVDC interconnections, and energy-storage systems — combined with strengthened technical expertise and local manufacturing capability. Continued investment in this field is therefore essential for building a cleaner, more resilient, and sustainable energy future for Bangladesh and the global community. To evaluate and analyze the performance of these controllers based on their Root Locus plots. 3. To adjust and optimize the PID controller parameters to achieve the desired system performance. Theory: Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR): The Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) is an optimal control strategy designed for linear systems to minimize a quadratic cost function, typically representing a trade-off between tracking performance and control energy. It provides a systematic methodology for calculating a feedback gain matrix K that ensures the stability and optimality of the system's state regulation or tracking [2]. Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID): A Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller is a three-term feedback mechanism that generates a control signal based on the error between a desired setpoint and a measured process variable [1]. 1. Proportional (P): Provides an action proportional to the current error. 2. Integral (I): Reduces steady-state error by accumulating past errors. 3. Derivative (D): Improves transient response by predicting future error based on its current rate of change [1]. 1 | P a g e Root Locus: The Root Locus method is a graphical technique used in control system design to show how the roots (poles) of the closed-loop characteristic equation move in the complex s-plane as a specific parameter, typically the loop gain $k$, varies from zero to infinity. It allows designers to evaluate system stability and transient performance visually by observing the trajectories of these poles. Trial and Error Method: In the context of LQR design, trial and error refers to the iterative process of manually adjusting the weighting matrices Q (state penalty) and R (control penalty) to meet specific performance criteria such as rise time, overshoot, or settling time [2]. Because the relationship between the weights in Q and R and the resulting time-domain performance is often non-linear and complex, designers frequently start with Bryson’s Rule or an identity matrix and then "tune" the diagonal elements until the system response is optimized [2]. To design a PID controller for the given systems using the trial-and-error method and to analyze and compare its performance characteristics Theory: PID control, representing proportional-integral-derivative control, is a feedback mechanism in control system, often referred to as three-term control. By adjusting three parameters—the proportional, integral, and derivative values of a process variable’s deviation from its set point—specific control actions are effectively tailored.[1] Proportional (P) response: The proportional gain (Kc) determines the ratio of output response to the error signal. In general, increasing the proportional gain will increase the speed of the control system response. Integral (I) response: The integral component sums the error term over time. The result is that even a small error term will cause the integral component to increase slowly. The integral response will continually increase over time unless the error is zero, so the effect is to drive the Steady-State error to zero. Derivative(D) response: The derivative component causes the output to decrease if the process variable is increasing rapidly. The derivative response is proportional to the rate of change of the process variable.[2] Some control actions only require two of the PID controller’s parameters, setting the third to zero. This flexibility allows PID controllers to operate as PI (proportional-integral), PD (proportional-derivative), or simply P or I. The proportional, derivative and integral parameters can be expressed as – Kp, Kd and Ki. All these three parameters have an effect on the closed loop control system. Core sizing equations for the inductor, input/output capacitors, sense and feedback resistors, as well as ripple and ripple-factor calculations, help set initial values and define performance targets before making adjustments [3]. Beyond the power stage and control loop, the design focuses on electromagnetic compatibility and practical manufacturability. High di/dt loop areas are minimized through careful PCB layout. Snubbers and clamps help reduce ringing. Conducted and radiated emissions are managed with filtering and measurement best practices. 1.2 Principle of Operation The operation of the boost converter is governed by the fundamental energy storage and release properties of an inductor. The circuit typically consists of four essential components: 1. An inductor (L) for energy storage. 2. A MOSFET (switch) for controlled energy transfer. 3. A diode (D) to enforce unidirectional current flow. 4. A capacitor (C) for voltage smoothing and load support. The working cycle can be explained in two modes: • Switch ON phase: When the MOSFET is turned ON, the input voltage is directly applied across the inductor. The inductor resists the sudden change in current, resulting in a gradual buildup of current and magnetic energy. During this period, the diode is reverse biased, isolating the load from the input. The load is powered solely by the capacitor. • Switch OFF phase: When the MOSFET is turned OFF, the inductor’s magnetic field collapses, releasing its stored energy. The polarity of the induced voltage reverses, forward biasing the diode. The inductor current, combined with the source voltage, charges the capacitor and supplies the load. The result is an output voltage greater than the input voltage. 1.3 Mathematical Relation In continuous conduction mode (CCM), where the inductor current never falls to zero, the steady-state voltage conversion ratio is given as: where: • Vin = input voltage • Vout = output voltage • D = duty cycle (fraction of time switch is ON) This equation shows that as the duty cycle increases, the output voltage rises. For instance, at a duty cycle of 0.75 (75%), the output theoretically reaches four times the input. However, in practical systems, factors such as diode forward voltage drop, MOSFET on-resistance, and inductor resistance reduce the achievable output. At higher duty cycles (>50%), stability becomes critical, requiring current-mode control with slope compensation to prevent subharmonic oscillations. By carefully selecting the inductance and capacitance, we ensured continuous conduction and limited output voltage ripple to within 1% of the rated voltage. • Semiconductor Device Selection: Understanding the role of switching devices was essential in choosing an appropriate MOSFET with low Rds(on) to minimize conduction losses, and a Schottky diode with low forward voltage drop to enhance efficiency. • Thermal and EMI Considerations: Familiarity with electromagnetic interference (EMI) sources and thermal effects allowed us to select switching frequencies and component ratings that balance efficiency with safe operation. It illustrates the link between theoretical analysis and practical implementation, ensuring that abstract design equations become a working hardware system capable of real-world performance. Thus, the development of the 9 V to 36 V boost converter demonstrates not only the mastery of fundamental concepts but also the capacity to apply them meaningfully in engineering practice. At each step, the feedback voltage was measured and compared with the desired reference. If the actual feedback voltage was lower than expected, the PWM duty cycle was incrementally increased, constrained within safe limits. Conversely, if the actual feedback was higher than expected, the duty cycle was decreased accordingly. When the actual and desired voltages were equal, the duty cycle remained unchanged. The updated PWM value was then applied to the switching MOSFET. This closed-loop adjustment ensured stable regulation of the output voltage. The algorithm for the control of the pulse width modulation of the boost converter can be described as: 1. Initialization: 1.1 Set feedback as INPUT. 1.2 Set PWM as OUTPUT. 1.3 Configure PWM frequency. 1.4 Initialize pwm with starting duty cycle. 2. Control Loop (repeat indefinitely): 2.1 Read actualFeedback ← analogRead(feedback). 2.2 If desiredFeedback > actualFeedback: a) Increase pwm ← pwm + 1. b) Constrain pwm within [pwm_min, pwm_max]. 2.3 Else if desiredFeedback < actualFeedback: a) Decrease pwm ← pwm – 1. b) Constrain pwm within [pwm_min, pwm_max]. 2.4 Else: keep pwm unchanged. 2.5 Apply control: analogWrite(PWM, pwm). 3. Repeat Step 2 continuously until system is stopped. 2.3 Circuit Diagram The proposed converter circuit consists of an IRFZ44N MOSFET as the switch, a Schottky diode (1N5819), a wound-core inductor, and an electrolytic output capacitor. The input is a 9 V DC supply, boosted to 36 V through switching action. The Arduino Nano provides PWM pulses at 32 kHz. 1.1 Introduction
A boost converter is a type of DC-to-DC converter that increases a low input voltage to a higher
output voltage. Its operation is based on the energy-storing property of an inductor. The circuit
consists of a single inductor, a controlled switch (MOSFET), a rectifier (diode), and a capacitor.
The conversion process is divided into two main stages, determined by the state of the switch.

Objective: 1. To observe the operation of a single-phase full-wave (center-tapped) rectifier with a resistive load. 2. To measure and calculate the DC output voltage (V ), RMS voltage (V ), DC RMS ripple factor, and form factor of the rectified signal. 3. To analyze the performance of the full-wave rectifier in terms of efficiency and output quality. Theory: A single-phase full-wave rectifier with a center-tapped transformer is an AC-to-DC conversion circuit that makes use of both the positive and negative halves of the input AC signal. The center-tapped transformer divides the input voltage into two equal and opposite voltages relative to the center tap, which serves as the reference point. Two diodes are arranged so that each one conducts during alternating half-cycles of the AC input, resulting in a rectified output with twice the frequency of the input signal. The output voltage of the rectifier can be expressed as, 2𝑉𝑚 V = DC 𝑛 Where V is the peak voltage of the transformer secondary winding. m The RMS voltage is given by, 𝑉𝑚 V = rms √2 The ripple factor measures the presence of AC components in the DC output and is defined as the ratio of the RMS value of the AC components to the DC value. In a full-wave rectifier, the ripple factor is lower compared to a half-wave rectifier, resulting in a more stable DC output [1]. A full-wave rectifier is also more efficient than a half-wave rectifier, achieving up to 81.2% efficiency under ideal conditions. Additionally, it requires a smaller filter to produce a smooth DC output, making it well-suited for applications that demand higher output quality [2]. The ripple factor, determined to be 48.34%, indicates a moderate level of ripple in the output signal—characteristic of full-wave rectification, though significantly lower than that of a half- wave rectifier. The form factor of 1.1107 suggests only slight variation between the RMS and DC values, confirming that the rectifier delivers a relatively stable DC output. With an efficiency of 81.06%, the rectifier aligns closely with the theoretical efficiency of a full-wave rectifier, demonstrating a notable improvement over a half-wave rectifier, which typically achieves around 40.5% efficiency. Conclusion: The experiment successfully validated the expected characteristics of a single-phase full-wave (center-tapped) rectifier. The output exhibited a moderate ripple factor alongside a high efficiency of 81.06%. Date of Experiment: December 09, 2024 Date of Submission: January 06, 2025 Title The Role of Power Electronics for Environmental Sustainability. Abstract Environmental sustainability has become a critical global concern, with the need to transition to cleaner energy sources and reduce carbon emissions being more urgent than ever. This report investigates the pivotal role of power electronics in achieving environmental sustainability. Power electronics, involving the efficient conversion, control, and management of electrical energy, is essential for integrating renewable energy sources, improving energy efficiency, and enabling sustainable transportation. This report will provide an overview of power electronics, its key features, and its applications in various sectors. It will also analyse relevant data, discuss future prospects, and present a perspective on the importance of power electronics in the context of Bangladesh's power sector. The findings highlight that power electronics is not just a technological advancement but a crucial driver for a sustainable future. Introduction Global warming, driven by the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, poses a significant threat to the planet. The International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has confirmed that human activities are the primary cause of the observed warming trend [1]. The consequences of inaction are severe, including rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and ecological disruptions. To mitigate these effects, a transition to sustainable energy sources and the adoption of energy-efficient technologies are imperative. Sustainable energy, derived from renewable sources like solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal, offers a viable solution to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels [2]. However, the intermittent nature of these sources necessitates advanced technologies for efficient energy conversion and grid integration. Power electronics emerges as a critical technology in this regard. It is the study and application of solid-state electronics for the conversion and control of electric power. Its importance lies in its ability to enhance the efficiency of energy use, facilitate the integration of renewable energy sources, and support the development of sustainable transportation systems [3]. Power electronics can withstand high power, with less current consumption, and controllability. It has been estimated that roughly 15%-20% of electricity. According to estimates, the extensive use of power electronics can reduce electricity consumption by between 15 and 20 percent. This report will delve into the role of power electronics in promoting environmental sustainability. It will explore the key features of power electronics, provide real-world examples and data, examine future trends, and discuss the specific implications for Bangladesh's power sector. Theory: A counter is one of the most fundamental and widely used building blocks in digital electronics. In digital systems, a counter is a sequential circuit that goes through a predefined sequence of states in response to an input clock signal. Counters are used in a vast array of applications including frequency division, event counting, digital clocks, timers, memory address generation, and control sequencing in microprocessors and microcontrollers. The basic building block of any counter is a flip-flop a bistable multivibrator that can store one bit of information and change its state in response to a triggering edge (rising or falling) of a clock signal. The most commonly used flip-flops in counter design are the JK flip-flop and the T (Toggle) flip-flop. A T flip-flop toggles its output on every active clock edge when T = 1, while a JK flip-flop offers SET, RESET, HOLD, and TOGGLE operations based on its J and K inputs. A 3-bit binary counter uses three flip-flops connected together and counts from 000 to 111 in binary (0 to 7 in decimal) for an up counter, or from 111 to 000 for a down counter. An up-down counter can count in both directions depending on a control input. The sequence of states each flip- flop output takes constitutes the state transition table of the counter, which is essential for analyzing its behavior. There are several types of counters used in digital design: asynchronous (ripple) counters, synchronous counters, decade counters, ring counters, Johnson counters, up/down counters, and modulus counters. Each type differs in the way clock pulses are applied, the speed of operation, and the complexity of design. This experiment focuses on synchronous and asynchronous 3-bit binary up/down counters. Asynchronous (Ripple) Counter: An asynchronous counter, also called a ripple counter, is a type of digital counter in which the flip- flops do not all share a common clock signal. Instead, only the first flip-flop (least significant bit) receives the external clock pulse. Each subsequent flip-flop in the chain uses the output Q of the previous flip-flop as its clock input.

Each subsequent flip-flop in the chain uses the output Q of the previous flip-flop as its clock input. As a result, the state change ripples through from one flip-flop to the next, one at a time hence the name “ripple counter.” Asynchronous counters are typically built using trailing-edge (negative-edge) triggered JK flip-flops, with J = K = 1 so that each flip- flop toggles on every falling edge of its clock input. The first flip-flop toggles every clock cycle; the second toggles every two clock cycles; the third toggles every four clock cycles. This creates the standard binary counting sequence. The key advantage of the asynchronous counter is its simplicity fewer connections and lower hardware complexity. However, because each flip-flop’s output triggers the next, there is a cumulative propagation delay. In high-speed systems, this delay can cause glitches and incorrect intermediate states called “spurious states.” For a 3-bit counter, if the propagation delay per flip-flop is t_pd, the total worst-case delay is 3 × t_pd. This limits the maximum operating frequency of ripple counters and makes them unsuitable for high-speed or timing-critical applications. 3-bit Asynchronous Up Counter: In a 3-bit asynchronous up counter, the counter starts at 000 and increments by 1 with each clock pulse, reaching a maximum of 111 (decimal 7) and then rolling back to 000. Each flip-flop toggles when the output of the preceding flip-flop transitions from HIGH to LOW (falling edge). Q0 is the LSB and Q2 is the MSB. Figure 1: 3-bit Asynchronous Up Counter 3-bit Asynchronous Down Counter: A 3-bit asynchronous down counter counts from 111 (decimal 7) down to 000 and then repeats. In this configuration, each flip-flop is clocked by the complement output Q̅ of the previous flip-flop rather than Q. This means the next flip-flop toggles when the previous output transitions from LOW to HIGH, producing a decrementing binary sequence. Figure 2: 3-bit Asynchronous Down Counter 3-bit Asynchronous Up-Down Counter: An asynchronous up-down counter combines both counting directions using a mode control input (M). When M = 0, the counter counts up by connecting Q outputs to subsequent flip-flop clocks. When M = 1, the counter counts down by connecting Q̅ outputs instead. Experiment No: 04
Experiment Name: Design and Implementation of a 3-bit Synchronous & Asynchronous

UP/DOWN Counter using Flip-Flops.

Objectives:

1. To understand the basic working principles of synchronous and asynchronous counters and the

fundamental differences between them.

2. To design and implement a 3-bit synchronous Up, Down, and Up-Down counter using T flip-

flops in MATLAB/Simulink or on a digital breadboard.

3. To design and implement a 3-bit asynchronous (ripple) Up, Down, and Up-Down counter

using JK flip-flops.

4. To analyze and compare the propagation delay and timing behavior of synchronous versus

asynchronous counters.

5. To construct the state transition table and timing diagrams for each counter type and verify the

counter sequence experimentally.

6. To evaluate the effect of clock signal on the triggering mechanism of each flip-flop in both

counter configurations.

7. To understand the role of T flip-flops and JK flip-flops in building binary counter circuits and

apply Boolean logic in counter design.

Theory:

A counter is one of the most fundamental and widely used building blocks in digital electronics.

In digital systems, a counter is a sequential circuit that goes through a predefined sequence of states

in response to an input clock signal. Counters are used in a vast array of applications including

frequency division, event counting, digital clocks, timers, memory address generation, and control

sequencing in microprocessors and microcontrollers.

The basic building block of any counter is a flip-flop a bistable multivibrator that can store one bit

of information and change its state in response to a triggering edge (rising or falling) of a clock

signal.  The  most  commonly  used  flip-flops  in  counter  design  are  the  JK  flip-flop  and  the  T

 (Toggle) flip-flop. A T flip-flop toggles its output on every active clock edge when T = 1, while a

JK flip-flop offers SET, RESET, HOLD, and TOGGLE operations based on i

text: at low operating frequencies. Importance of Synchronous Counters: Synchronous counters are the backbone of high-speed digital systems. Because all flip-flops are clocked simultaneously, there is no accumulated propagation delay, which allows synchronous counters to operate at significantly higher frequencies than asynchronous ones. This makes them indispensable in modern processors, FPGAs, digital signal processors, and high-speed communication systems. Synchronous counters also avoid the spurious intermediate states (glitches) that occur in ripple counters, which is crucial in systems where incorrect transient states could trigger unintended operations. Comparison Summary: In summary, asynchronous counters are valued for their simplicity and low-cost implementation in slow, non-critical applications, while synchronous counters are essential for fast, reliable, and precise digital operations. The choice between the two depends on the speed requirement, acceptable delay, hardware complexity, and the timing sensitivity of the target application. A thorough understanding of both counter types gives a digital designer the flexibility to make optimal design decisions in real-world engineering scenarios. Discussion: This experiment involved designing 3-bit synchronous and asynchronous up/down counters using flip-flops. The asynchronous counter, built with JK flip-flops, showed ripple delays due to sequential clocking. Each flip-flop received its clock from the previous stage’s output, which introduced a cumulative propagation delay across the three stages. Conclusion: The experiment successfully demonstrated the design and operation of both 3-bit synchronous and asynchronous up/down counters. Synchronous counters implemented with T flip-flops provided accurate, glitch-free, and stable outputs by sharing a common clock, making them more reliable for high-speed applications. Asynchronous counters implemented with JK flip-flops, while simpler in design, exhibited the characteristic ripple delay that limits their use in timing-critical systems. Overall, the experiment improved understanding of digital counter design, ff behavior, the comparative timing characteristics of synchronous versus asynchronous sequential circuits. Theory: A single-phase full-wave rectifier with a center-tapped transformer is an AC-to-DC conversion circuit that makes use of both the positive and negative halves of the input AC signal. The center-tapped transformer divides the input voltage into two equal and opposite voltages relative to the center tap, which serves as the reference point. Two diodes are arranged so that each one conducts during alternating half-cycles of the AC input, resulting in a rectified output with twice the frequency of the input signal. In a full-wave rectifier, the ripple factor is lower compared to a half-wave rectifier, resulting in a more stable DC output [1]. A full-wave rectifier is also more efficient than a half-wave rectifier, achieving up to 81.2% efficiency under ideal conditions. Additionally, it requires a smaller filter to produce a smooth DC output, making it well-suited for applications that demand higher output quality [2]. Hafiz Ahamed Roll:2208053 Assistant Professor MTE, RUET MTE, RUET Sarafat Hussain Abhi Assistant Professor MTE, RUET Date of Experiment: Date of Submission: Experiment No: 05 Experiment Name: Design and Implementation of SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO, Johnson, Ring counters in Logisim. Objectives: • Understand the fundamental operations of different types of shift registers (SISO, SIPO, PISO, and PIPO) and counters (Johnson, Ring), as well as their roles in sequential digital circuits. • Design logic circuits for each type of shift register and counter using flip-flops and the required combinational logic components. • Implement and simulate the designed circuits using Logisim software to verify their theoretical functionality. Theory: A register is a group of flip-flops, each sharing a common clock and capable of storing one bit of information. An n-bit register consists of a group of n flip-flops capable of storing n bits of binary information. In addition to the flip-flops, a register may feature combinational gates that perform specific data-processing tasks. In its broadest definition, a register consists of a group of flip-flops combined with gates that dictate how information is transferred into the register. A register capable of shifting its stored binary information to its neighboring cell in a selected direction is called a shift register. The logical configuration of a shift register consists of a chain of cascaded flip-flops, with the output of one flip-flop connected to the input of the next. All flip- flops receive common clock pulses, which activate the shift of data from one stage to the next. [1] SISO Shift Register: The SISO shift register is the most basic form of data shifting circuit. It accepts binary data serially (one bit at a time) through a single input pin and shifts it out serially through a single output pin. Internally, the output of each flip-flop connects directly to the input of the successive one. Because data must pass through every single flip-flop in the chain, it requires n clock pulses to fully load an n-bit word into the register, and another n clock pulses to shift it out completely. While this makes the SISO register relatively slow for data transfer, it is incredibly useful as a digital delay line. By adjusting the clock frequency or the number of flip-flops in the cascade, engineers can introduce a precise time delay into a digital signal, allowing it to act as a synchronized buffer between asynchronous devices. Like the SISO register, data is fed into the system serially, bit by bit, requiring n clock cycles to load an n-bit word. However, the key structural difference is that the outputs of every flip-flop are externally accessible simultaneously. Once the entire data string has been clocked into the register, the complete binary word can be read across the parallel output lines all at once. This configuration is widely used in communication systems (such as UART receivers) where data is transmitted over a single wire to save space, but needs to be processed by a microprocessor in parallel chunks (like 8-bit bytes) for faster internal computation. It takes parallel data from multiple input lines and transmits it out sequentially over a single output line. To achieve this, the PISO register utilizes a control signal typically called "Shift/Load". When this control line is set to the "Load" state, combinational logic (such as multiplexers) bypasses the shifting mechanism, allowing all n bits of input data to be jammed into the flip-flops simultaneously on a single clock pulse. Once the data is loaded, the control line is switched to "Shift", and subsequent clock pulses push the stored data out of the final flip-flop sequentially. Sakib Hassan Chowdhury Lecturer Department of Mechatronics Engineering Rajshahi University of Engineering & Technology, Rajshahi-6204. | ***Date of Experiment: 1st June, 2024*** ***Date of Submission: 29th June, 2024*** **MTE 3104** **Microcontroller and Interfacing Sessional** **Experiment No.:** 08 **Experiment Name:** 1Hz Signal Generation using Atmega32 (Timer0) with Proteus Simulation. **Objectives:** 1. To configure the Atmega32 microcontroller for generating a 1Hz signal using Timer0. 2. To simulate the 1Hz signal generation using Proteus software. 3. To understand the process of setting up Timer0 on the Atmega32. 4. To verify the accuracy and stability of the generated 1Hz signal through simulation. 5. To demonstrate the practical application of microcontroller timers in signal generation. **Theory:** Timers are integral peripherals in microcontrollers used for counting and timing applications. The Atmega32 microcontroller features several timers, including Timer0, an 8-bit timer. The timer can be configured to operate in various modes, such as Normal, CTC (Clear Timer on Compare Match), Fast PWM, and Phase Correct PWM. To generate a 1Hz signal, the CTC mode of Timer0 can be used. In CTC mode, the timer counter (TCNT0) counts from 0 to a specified value stored in the Output Compare Register (OCR0). Introduction: Digital electronics form the bedrock of modern computing, communication, and control architectures. At the core of these systems are logic gates, which are the fundamental building blocks that execute basic Boolean operations required for sophisticated electronic design. To effectively bridge theoretical logic concepts with real-world applications, practical circuit implementation is strictly necessary. This experiment investigates the operation of the primary logic gates (7408 (AND), 7432 (OR), 7404 (NOT), 7400 (NAND), 7402 (NOR), 7486(XOR), 74266(XNOR)) using 74-series Transistor-Transistor Logic (TTL) integrated circuits. The TTL ICs utilized in this lab encapsulate multiple independent logic gates within a single package. By physically wiring these components on a breadboard, applying +5V DC regulated power, and monitoring output states via LED indicators, theoretical truth tables are empirically verified. This hands-on methodology not only demonstrates the functional realities of digital logic but also establishes a foundational skill set for designing more complex architectures like arithmetic logic units (ALUs), multiplexers, and memory registers. In this laboratory experiment, these logic gates are implemented and tested on a breadboard, allowing circuit construction without permanent soldering. This hands-on approach helps students understand the practical operation of logic gates and their role in building larger digital systems such as multiplexers, adders, and flip-flops. The output of each gate is displayed using an LED connected through a current-limiting resistor, while a regulated +5 V DC supply provides the operating voltage required for TTL devices. Jumper wires are used to establish the necessary circuit connections between the ICs, power source, and ground. Through the successful implementation and testing of these logic gates, students gain practical experience in circuit assembly, verification, and troubleshooting. Functionally, it operates as an AND gate immediately followed by an inverter. Its "universal" designation stems from the fact that any digital logic circuit can be synthesized using NAND gates alone. The IC 7402 facilitates this with four independent 2-input NOR gates. Fig 5: NOR Gate 6. XOR Gate (IC 7486): The Exclusive-OR (XOR) gate serves as a digital inequality detector. It generates a HIGH (1) output only when its inputs are at differing logic levels (e.g., one HIGH, one LOW). If the inputs match, the output is LOW. Sakib Hassan Chowdhury Lecturer, Department of Mechatronics, RUET , , Date of Submission: 20/1/2026 Date of Experiment: 13/1/2026 Experiment No.: 2 Experiment Name: Implementation of a NAND Logic Gate Using ATmega32 Microcontroller Objectives: • To study the basic architecture of the AVR ATmega32 microcontroller. • To understand the function of I/O ports in the ATmega32. • To write and execute a C program to control LEDs connected to PORTC using NAND gate at PORTD. • To understand the logical operation of a NAND gate, to implement digital logic using a microcontroller, and to verify the NAND truth table using hardware simulation. Apparatus Required: • Proteus Simulation Software • Atmel Studio Introduction: Digital logic gates are the fundamental building blocks of digital electronics and computer systems. Among all logic gates, the NAND gate holds special importance because it is a universal gate, meaning that any other logic gate or digital circuit can be constructed using only NAND gates [1]. Microcontrollers such as the ATmega32 provide a flexible platform for implementing digital logic functions through software, eliminating the need for discrete logic ICs and enabling rapid prototyping [2]. In this experiment, an ATmega32 microcontroller is used to implement a NAND gate by reading two digital inputs from push-button switches and producing the corresponding output on an LED. The logic operation is performed programmatically inside the microcontroller, demonstrating the use of embedded systems for digital logic realization. Theory: A NAND gate performs the logical NOT of the AND operation. The ATmega32 is an 8-bit AVR microcontroller featuring 32 programmable I/O pins, which can be configured as either inputs or outputs through software registers [2]. By reading the state of two input pins connected to switches and controlling an output pin connected to an LED, the NAND logic function can be implemented entirely in software. The output of the NAND gate is LOW only when both inputs are HIGH; otherwise, the output remains HIGH [1]. Objectives:

•  To study the basic architecture of the AVR ATmega32 microcontroller.
•  To understand the function of I/O ports in the ATmega32.
•  To write and execute a C program to control LEDs connected to PORTC using NAND

gate at PORTD.

•  To understand the logical operation of a NAND gate, to implement digital logic using a

microcontroller, and to verify the NAND truth table using hardware simulation.

Apparatus Required:

•  Proteus Simulation Software
•  Atmel Studio

Introduction:
Digital  logic  gates  are  the  fundamental  building  blocks  of  digital  electronics  and  computer
systems.  Among  all  logic  gates,  the  NAND  gate  holds  special  importance  because  it  is  a
universal gate, meaning that any other logic gate or digital circuit can be constructed using only
NAND  gates  [1].  Microcontrollers  such  as  the  ATmega32  provide  a  flexible  platform  for
implementing digital logic functions through software, eliminating the need for discrete logic
ICs and  enabling rapid  prototyping [2].  In this experiment,  an ATmega32 microcontroller is
used to implement a NAND gate by reading two digital inputs from push-button switches and
producing  the  corresponding  output  on  an  LED.  The  logic  operation  is  performed
programmatically inside the microcontroller, demon

text: input while (1) { if ( (PIND & (1<<PD0)) && !(PIND & (1<<PD1)) ) { PORTC = 0b00000001; // LED ON } else if ( !(PIND & (1<<PD0)) && (PIND & (1<<PD1)) ) { PORTC = 0b00000001; // LED ON } else if ((PIND & (1<<PD0)) && (PIND & (1<<PD1)) ) { PORTC = 0b00000000; // LED OFF } else { PORTC = 0b00000001; // LED ON } } return 0; } Circuit Description: The circuit consists of an ATmega32 microcontroller, two SPST switches used as logic inputs, two pull-down resistors to ensure stable logic levels, and an LED connected as the output indicator. The switches are connected to digital input pins of the microcontroller, while the LED is connected to a digital output pin through a current-limiting resistor. When the switches are pressed or released, the microcontroller reads the input states and computes the NAND operation, updating the LED state accordingly. Fig 2: Circuit Diagram of NAND Gate in Proteus Workings: When the circuit is powered, the ATmega32 continuously monitors the logic levels of the two input pins connected to the switches. These inputs represent logic ‘0’ when the switch is open and logic ‘1’ when the switch is pressed. The microcontroller executes a NAND logic operation in software. If both inputs are HIGH, the output pin is driven LOW, turning the LED OFF. For all other input combinations, the output pin is driven HIGH, turning the LED ON. This behavior confirms the correct operation of the NAND gate. Result: Fig 3: When two switches are OFF Fig 4: When switch 1 is ON Fig 5: When switch 2 is ON Fig 6: When two switch is ON The experimental results confirm that the implemented circuit behaves as a NAND gate. The LED remains ON for all input combinations except when both switches are pressed simultaneously, at which point the LED turns OFF. This verifies the logical expression 𝑌 = 𝐴 ⋅ 𝐵‾ . Discussion: The experiment demonstrates that microcontrollers can effectively replace traditional logic gate ICs in digital system design. Implementing logic functions through software provides greater flexibility, reduces hardware complexity, and allows easy modification of logic behaviour without changing physical components. However, compared to dedicated logic ICs, microcontroller-based logic may introduce slight processing delays and requires proper programming knowledge. Conclusion: In this experiment, a NAND gate was successfully implemented using an ATmega32 microcontroller, two switches, and an LED. The circuit operation was verified through Proteus simulation, and the observed results matched the theoretical NAND gate truth table. The experiment highlights the versatility of microcontrollers in digital logic applications and reinforces the fundamental concept of universal logic gates. References 1. M. Morris Mano and M. D. This is accomplished using a diode, which acts as a one-way switch. During the positive half-
cycle of the AC input, the diode is forward-biased, allowing current to pass through, whereas
in the negative half-cycle, it becomes reverse-biased and prevents current flow. Consequently,
only the positive half of the waveform reaches the output, while the negative half is blocked,
producing a pulsating DC output [1].

Key Features of Power Electronics Power electronics systems offer several key features that contribute to environmental sustainability. High Power Electronics: Advances in high-power electronics, particularly using wide- bandgap materials, are revolutionizing the electrical power system. These devices can operate at higher temperatures and voltages, leading to increased efficiency and reduced losses in power transmission and distribution. Energy Efficiency: Power electronics enables significant energy savings across various applications. By precisely controlling the speed of motors, pumps, and fans, power electronics optimizes energy consumption in industrial processes and building systems. Hybrid and electric vehicles, powered by power electronics, offer substantial reductions in fuel consumption and emissions. Integration of Renewable Energy: Power electronics plays a vital role in integrating intermittent renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, into the electrical grid [4]. Power converters adjust the voltage and frequency of renewable energy output to match grid requirements, ensuring stable and reliable power supply. Flexible Control: Power electronics provides advanced control capabilities for managing complex energy systems. This includes load balancing in smart grids, optimizing energy storage, and enabling the integration of distributed generation sources. More Flexible Control by Power Electronics: Power electronics essentially employs high- efficiency switching power semiconductors to convert and control electrical power using dc- to-dc, dc-to-ac, ac-to-dc, and ac-to-ac converters, which are widely used in industrial, commercial, residential, transportation, aerospace, military, and utility systems. Data and Applications The positive impact of power electronics on environmental sustainability is evident in various sectors. Smart Grids: Smart grids utilize power electronics to dynamically manage electricity demand, storage, and supply. They enhance the efficiency of renewable energy integration, reduce transmission losses, and improve grid stability. Green Industries: Industries are increasingly adopting power electronics to minimize their carbon footprint. Applications include energy-efficient motor drives, power factor correction, and the integration of on-site renewable energy generation. Electric and Hybrid Vehicles: The growth of electric and hybrid vehicles relies heavily on power electronics for battery management, motor control, and regenerative braking. These vehicles offer significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional vehicles. Electric Aircraft: Power electronics is enabling the development of electric propulsion systems for aircraft, paving the way for cleaner and quieter air travel. Submitted by: Adiba Binta Newaz 2108043 Date of Submission: 19th April, 2025 Experiment No: 02 Experiment Name: Design of Open Loop System and Investigate the Performance. Objectives: To design an open-loop system for a given plant or process. To simulate or implement the designed system using appropriate tools (e.g., MATLAB, Simulink). To analyze the system performance parameters such as rise time, steady-state error, and system stability. Theory: An open-loop control system is a type of control system in which the output has no influence on the control action. It operates solely based on the input signal and the system’s predefined behavior, without using feedback to compare the actual output to the desired output. Unlike closed-loop systems, there is no mechanism to correct errors or respond to external disturbances in open-loop systems. The system assumes the relationship between input and output remains consistent over time. Figure 1: Open loop system diagram.[1] Key Features of open loop control system: a. No feedback loop = output is not measured or used for correction. b. Simple design = fewer components and easy to implement. c. Low cost = ideal for systems where precision is not critical. d. Less accurate = due to lack of error correction from feedback. e. Fast response = no time is spent in measuring output or adjusting. Performance Characteristics of Open Loop Systems: 1. Rise Time (T ): The rise time is determined by the system's inherent dynamics and the input signal. r It is not adjusted based on the output since there's no feedback. 2. To program the ATmega8, an Arduino Uno can be used as an In-System Programmer (ISP). This method allows the microcontroller to be programmed directly within a circuit without removing it. By uploading the ArduinoISP sketch through the Arduino IDE and connecting the appropriate SPI pins between the Arduino Uno and the ATmega8, users can easily burn bootloaders or upload programs. This approach is cost-effective and convenient, especially for prototyping and educational purposes, as it eliminates the need for dedicated programming hardware. It typically consists of an IR emitter and a receiver that work together to detect reflected infrared light from nearby objects. When an object comes within range, the emitted infrared light reflects back to the receiver, causing a change in the sensor’s output signals. Step 3: As I’m linux user I needed to install avr-gcc to compile C code of ATmega8, avr- objcopy to make a runnable script on ATmega8 and last avr-dude to upload and burn ATmega8. All the script I have bult as run.sh and the ATmega code as main.c. Step 4: Run the script and it uploaded the main.c in ATmega8 and LED was on. Code: run.sh: avr-gcc -mmcu=atmega8 -DF_CPU=1000000UL -Os -o counter.elf main.c avr-objcopy -O ihex -R .eeprom counter.elf counter.hex avrdude -c stk500v1 -p m8 -P /dev/ttyACM0 -b 19200 -B 250 -U flash:w:counter.hex:i main.c: #include <avr/io.h> int main(void) { // Set PB1 and PB2 as output (LEDs) DDRB |= (1 << PB1) | (1 << PB2); // Set PB0 as input (IR sensor) DDRB &= ~(1 << PB0); while (1) { if (PINB & (1 << PB0)){ // Object detected PORTB |= (1 << PB1); // LED1 ON PORTB &= ~(1 << PB2); // LED2 OFF }else{ // No object PORTB |= (1 << PB2); // LED2 ON PORTB &= ~(1 << PB1); // LED1 OFF } } } Result: Fig 4: When no object is detected (Color LED) Fig 5:When object is detected (White) Discussion: In this experiment, the ATmega8 microcontroller was successfully programmed using Arduino Uno as an ISP, demonstrating a practical and low-cost programming method. The IR sensor was interfaced as a digital input device, providing HIGH or LOW signals depending on object presence. Based on the sensor output, two LEDs were controlled using conditional logic. The system behaved as expected: when an object was detected, LED1 turned ON, indicating detection, while LED2 turned OFF. In the absence of an object, LED2 remained ON continuously, serving as a default state indicator. This confirms proper interfacing of input and output devices and validates the logic implemented in the program. Conclusion: The experiment successfully demonstrated the use of Arduino Uno as an ISP to program the ATmega8 microcontroller. It also showed how an IR sensor can be used for object detection and how microcontroller pins can be used to control output devices like LEDs. The results confirm that embedded systems can be effectively built using simple components and basic programming techniques. Both curves fall steadily as the firing angle increases, confirming that a larger firing delay reduces the conduction period of the thyristors and hence the average output voltage. ![](data:image/png;base64...) *Figure 2. DC output voltage (calculated and observed) versus average firing angle.* The observed Vdc is consistently slightly lower than the calculated value at small firing angles, mainly due to voltage drops across the conducting thyristors and diodes, transformer/source impedance, and meter loading, which are neglected in the ideal formula. Figure 3 shows that the form factor increases steadily with firing angle, rising from about 1.13 at minimum firing angle to 1.36 at 80°, indicating that the ripple content of the output waveform increases as the conduction angle is reduced. ![](data:image/png;base64...) *Figure 3. Form factor (Vrms/Vdc) versus average firing angle.* The percentage error between the calculated and observed DC voltages remained small (under about 4.1%) across all firing angles, showing good agreement between theory and the experimental hardware, with the free-wheeling action of diodes D1 and D2 helping to maintain a well-defined output waveform throughout the firing-angle range tested. # **Conclusion** The single-phase full-wave semi-converter using thyristors T1, T2 and diodes D1, D2 was successfully constructed and tested. The DC output voltage was found to decrease with increasing firing angle, in close agreement with the theoretical relationship Vdc = (Vm/2π)[2 + cosα1 + cosα2]. The form factor increased with firing angle, confirming greater ripple content at higher delay angles. The small deviations between calculated and observed values (2.7-4.1%) can be attributed to practical non-idealities such as device voltage drops and source impedance. Overall, the experiment confirmed that the firing angle of the thyristors provides an effective means of controlling the DC output voltage of a full-wave rectifier. **Reference:** [1] M. H. This enables precise duty cycle control and creates opportunities for further system enhancements such as closed-loop regulation, monitoring, and digital control strategies. The development of this converter not only strengthens our understanding of fundamental power electronics concepts but also bridges the gap between theoretical classroom knowledge and real-world implementation. 1.2 Relevance of Power Electronics in the Project This project is a direct application of power electronics knowledge to solve a practical engineering challenge. The load and input voltage variations will lead to output voltage variations. A feedback control system is employed for counteracting this. The system varies the duty cycle adaptively for a stable output of 24V, enabling the converter consistently to accommodate variations in the input or in the load conditions. This real-time correction is essential for the converter output stability and shows the need for feedback control for a successful power electronic design. 3.3 Thermal Management The high duty cycle also increases the component stress, especially that of MOSFET and inductor, and results in more power dissipation and overheating. Proper thermal management has to be done in order to prevent component failure due to excessive heating. Heat sinking and efficient design of a PCB are also essential in enabling the components to remain at safe temperatures. Efficient heat dissipation also makes the converter reliable for Page | 13 long periods of usage, particularly in real-world applications where thermal stress is a serious issue. 3.4 Optimization and Trade-offs Whereas design at a theoretical level creates a basis, practical applications very often require compromise. The selection of switching frequency, for example, has a direct bearing both on efficiency and component packaging. Higher switching frequencies minimize component packaging at the expense of increased switching loss, and a delicate balance has to be struck for a desired performance. Likewise, PWM control integration using ESP32 gives highly accurate duty cycle adjustments for optimized performance and ease of adjustments and monitoring. This identifies that there need to be both analog and digital solutions for today's power electronics design applications that need accurate control and efficiency. 3.5 Conclusion Contextual reasoning for Boost Converter design stresses the importance of applying practical constraints to theoretical knowledge. By employing the appropriate components, real-time control of voltage, thermal control, and optimization of system performance by trade-off, the converter can efficiently and reliably function. Introduction Logisim is a free, open-source digital logic circuit simulator developed by Carl Burch that allows users to design, test, and debug digital circuits on a computer using a simple drag-and- drop graphical interface. It is widely used in universities and for self-learning in digital electronics because it enables building circuits from basic gates up to complex systems such as adders, multiplexers, RAM, and even simple CPUs without any physical hardware. The software provides real-time simulation, truth tables, timing diagrams, and error highlighting, and it supports both combinational and sequential logic. Flip-flops are fundamental bistable multivibrator circuits in digital electronics that can store one bit of binary information. Unlike combinational circuits, flip-flops are sequential circuits whose output depends not only on the present input but also on the previous state. They are the basic building blocks of registers, counters, memory units, and finite state machines. This experiment investigates five major types of flip-flops — SR, JK, Master-Slave, D, and T — each with distinct input characteristics and state-transition behavior. Understanding these devices is essential for designing stable and efficient digital systems. It has two inputs Set (S) and Reset (R) which control the output Q. When S=1 and R=0, the output is set to logic high; when S=0 and R=1, the output is reset to logic low. The condition S=1, R=1 is considered an invalid or forbidden state in NOR-based implementation, as it creates an indeterminate output. text: flop JK Flip-Flop The JK flip-flop is an enhanced version of the SR flip-flop that eliminates the invalid state problem. Its inputs J and K correspond to Set and Reset, respectively. When both J=1 and K=1 are applied simultaneously, the output toggles to its complement on each clock pulse, a condition not possible in the SR flip-flop. This toggle feature makes the JK flip-flop highly versatile for use in counters and frequency dividers. Its predictable behavior for all input combinations makes it one of the most widely used flip-flops in practical digital circuit design. Master-Slave JK Flip-Flop Fig 2: JK Flip Flop The Master-Slave flip-flop is a cascade arrangement of two JK flip-flops — a master stage and a slave stage — controlled by complementary clock signals. When the clock is high, the master captures the input data; when the clock goes low, the slave transfers the master's output to the final output terminals. This two-stage mechanism effectively eliminates the racing problem or clock skew that occurs in simple edge-triggered designs. The Master-Slave configuration ensures that output changes occur only once per clock cycle, making it particularly suitable for synchronous sequential circuit applications. D Flip-Flop/Data Flip-Flop Fig 3: Master Slave JK Flip Flop The D flip-flop, also known as the Data or Delay flip-flop, has a single data input D and transfers its value to the output Q on the active edge of the clock signal. It was designed to overcome the indeterminate state problem of the SR flip-flop by ensuring the two inputs are always complementary. The output simply follows the input after one clock cycle, acting as a one-bit delay element. D flip-flops are extensively used in shift registers, data latches, pipeline stages, and digital communication systems where data synchronization and temporary storage are required. Toggle (T) Flip-Flop Fig 4: D flip flop The T flip-flop, or Toggle flip-flop, has a single input T that controls whether the output toggles or remains unchanged. When T=0, the output retains its previous state; when T=1, the output complements itself on each clock edge. It is essentially a JK flip-flop with both inputs tied together. This toggling property makes the T flip-flop ideal for binary counter design, frequency division, and clock pulse generation circuits. A chain of T flip-flops with T=1 forms a ripple counter, dividing the input frequency by successive powers of two at each stage. Discussion Fig 5: T flip flop The experiment was conducted successfully, and the truth tables of all five flip-flop types were verified. However, several difficulties were encountered during the wiring process. Due to the large number of connections involved, incorrect pin connections were made initially, which produced unexpected output values. The breadboard connections were found to be loose at multiple points, causing intermittent signal failures. Power supply fluctuations were also observed, which temporarily affected the circuit behavior. After careful rewiring and re- checking of all connections against the circuit diagrams, stable and correct outputs were eventually obtained for each flip-flop configuration. The design demonstrates how theoretical principles translate into a practical solution that ensures stable and reliable voltage stepping for real-world applications. 1.2 Fundamentals of DC-DC Converters DC–DC converters are widely used in systems where the available DC voltage does not match the load requirements. They can be categorized into buck (step-down), boost (step-up), buck– boost (step-up/down), and isolated types such as flyback or forward converters. Among these, the boost converter is a non-isolated type that employs a switching device, inductor, diode, and capacitor to step up the input voltage. Its operation depends on pulse-width modulation (PWM), where the duty cycle of the switch regulates the energy stored and released by the inductor, thereby controlling the output voltage. DC-DC converters are generally classified into several types: i. Buck converters (step-down): Reduce the input voltage to a lower output voltage. ii. Boost converters (step-up): Increase the input voltage to a higher level. iii. Buck–boost converters: Can both step up or step down the voltage, depending on the duty cycle. iv. Isolated converters (e.g., flyback, forward): Provide electrical isolation between input and output using transformers, which makes them suitable for safety-critical and high-voltage applications. In ideal conditions, the energy balance in the inductor ensures efficient power transfer. Real- world implementations must account for parasitic elements, such as inductor resistance and diode forward voltage drop, which impact performance. 1.3 Boost Converter Operation The boost converter, which is the primary focus of this project, is a non-isolated topology that steps up the input voltage using four essential components: a switching device (usually a MOSFET), an inductor, a diode, and a capacitor. A boost converter operates in two primary phases: the switch-on (charging) and switch-off (discharging) periods. 3 i. Boost converters play a critical role in enabling efficient energy utilization in these systems. 3.1.3 Portable Devices: Battery-powered devices such as laptops, LED drivers, and mobile chargers rely on boost converters to maintain stable operation amid fluctuating input voltages [2]. On the positive side, the high efficiency achieved-potentially improved to match the 91% peak in referenced multicell designs [3] reduces energy dissipation as heat, lowering overall power consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. For example, in renewable systems, this efficiency can amplify the effective output from clean sources, displacing coal or gas-based electricity and contributing to carbon neutrality goals. The project's emphasis on voltage regulation and ripple minimization also ensures longer component lifespans, reducing the frequency of replacements and associated resource extraction. However, environmental challenges arise from manufacturing and disposal. Components like inductors and capacitors involve mining rare earth metals and producing electronic waste, which can leach toxins if not recycled properly. The MOSFET (IRFZ44N) and diodes in the design, while efficient, contribute to the semiconductor industry's high water and energy use during fabrication. Additionally, if not optimized, switching losses could lead to thermal inefficiencies, indirectly increasing cooling demands and energy use. The report's future recommendations, such as using low-resistance inductors and precise PWM control, mitigate these issues by enhancing durability and efficiency, but lifecycle analysis is essential. Overall, with proper e-waste management and eco-friendly sourcing, the net impact leans positive, especially in large-scale sustainable deployments. 4.5 Summary This chapter has underscored the boost converter's potential in fostering sustainability through applications in renewable energy, electric vehicles, and portable electronics, while critically evaluating its environmental footprint. The introduction set the stage for its relevance in eco- conscious engineering, followed by detailed explorations of how the project's design supports efficient energy use in variable renewable sources and battery systems. The environmental assessment revealed efficiency-driven emission reductions as a major benefit, tempered by manufacturing and waste concerns that can be addressed through optimizations like those suggested in the report. Objectives:  To understand the basic working environment, components, and simulation procedure of FluidSIM software.  To study the working principle of pneumatic logic valves used to realize Boolean logic operations.  To verify the output response of each simulated circuit against its corresponding truth table. Introduction: FluidSIM is a specialized simulation software, developed by Festo Didactic in cooperation with the Universities of Paderborn and Kaiserslautern that is used for the design, simulation, and analysis of pneumatic, hydraulic, and electro-pneumatic circuits. The software provides a graphical drag-and-drop environment in which standard ISO-symbol components, including compressors, directional control valves, cylinders, sensors, and logic valves, can be selected, interconnected, and animated to observe the dynamic behavior of a circuit under simulated operating conditions. Pneumatic systems form one of the oldest and most widely used branches of automation technology, in which compressed air is employed as the working medium to transmit energy and signals for the performance of mechanical work. Long before the advent of electronic and digital controllers, pneumatic components such as directional control valves, cylinders, and logic valves were combined to build control circuits capable of performing switching and decision-making functions analogous to those carried out by electronic logic gates. The fundamental Boolean operations, namely AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, and Exclusive-OR (X-OR), can each be physically realized through an appropriate arrangement of pneumatic valves, and such circuits remain relevant in industrial environments where explosion hazards, electromagnetic interference, moisture, or extreme temperatures make electrical control systems unsuitable. In this report I have discussed and displayed how FluidSIM was employed to design and simulate pneumatic circuits corresponding to the AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, and X-OR logic operations, and the response of each circuit was verified against its respective truth table. Building Logic Gates: 1. OR Gate: The OR logic gate was constructed in FluidSIM by using two pneumatic input lines connected to a shuttle valve (OR valve). The two inputs were designated as A and B, while the output was connected to a pneumatic actuator or indicator. Compressed air was supplied to both input lines through separate 3/2-way push-button valves. The outputs of these valves were connected to the two input ports of the shuttle valve. When either input valve was actuated, compressed air was allowed to pass through the shuttle valve to the output. The same response was obtained when both input valves were actuated simultaneously. Thus, the output became active when A or B or both were active, satisfying the Boolean expression Y = A + B. Figure-01: OR gate. 2. AND Gate: The AND logic gate was constructed by connecting two pneumatic input valves in such a way that compressed air had to pass through both valves before reaching the output.
